hints: Focus on what happens on heating, solid aluminium chloride turns into separate $Al_2Cl_6$ molecules that can sublime, which tells you a lot about the bonding.
Remember each $Al$ in $AlCl_3$ has only 6 electrons in its outer shell, so look for how a $Cl$ lone pair from a neighbour can fill that gap.
Sort the bonds into normal shared-pair $Al-Cl$ bonds and bridging bonds where $Cl$ donates both electrons, then see which pair of bond types that gives.
walkthrough:
**Compare solid and vapour**

Think like a detective. Ionic lattices have very high melting points and do not form small molecules. Since heating gives discrete $Al_2Cl_6$ molecules that sublime easily, the bonding in the vapour must be covalent, not ionic.

$$\text{solid lattice } AlCl_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \text{covalent dimer } Al_2Cl_6$$

**Spot why Al wants to dimerise**

Aluminium is in Group 13, so in $AlCl_3$ it has only 3 shared pairs, just 6 electrons. That is electron deficient and unstable. It really wants one more pair to complete its octet.

**See the two types of covalent bond**

In the dimer, each $Al$ makes two normal terminal covalent bonds where $Al$ and $Cl$ each supply one electron. Then two bridging $Cl$ atoms use a lone pair to form a co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond to the other $Al$, donating both electrons.

$$Al-Cl \text{ (normal covalent) + } Cl \rightarrow Al \text{ (dative covalent)}$$

**Conclude the bonding**

So $Al_2Cl_6$ contains both ordinary covalent bonds and co-ordinate bonds, all within covalent molecules. That matches covalent and co-ordinate (dative covalent).

options.A: Correct. $Al_2Cl_6$ is a covalent dimer. It has four terminal $Al-Cl$ normal covalent bonds and two bridging $Cl$ atoms that each form one normal covalent bond plus one dative bond to the second $Al$.
options.B: Close but incomplete. Students choose this by remembering $Al_2Cl_6$ is covalent and forgetting the bridges are special. The bridging bonds are formed by $Cl$ donating a lone pair into the empty orbital on $Al$, which is dative covalent.
options.C: Incorrect. This mixes up the solid with the dimer. Solid $AlCl_3$ has significant ionic character in its layer lattice, but once heated to $Al_2Cl_6$ the bonding becomes covalent. There is no ionic bonding in the discrete dimer.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the trap of thinking Group 1 style metal plus non-metal always means ionic. $Al^{3+}$ is small and highly polarising, so it polarises $Cl^-$ strongly, and $Al_2Cl_6$ exists as neutral covalent molecules with low sublimation temperature.
